newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia electricity reforms similar to U.K.- S&P.
newsitem.headline: Australia electricity reforms similar to U.K.- S&P.

text.p: Australia's electricity market reforms were following a similar path to that in the U.K. and were going about it in a better fashion, but the market has yet to reach a mature stage, Standard and Poor's Corp said.

Michael Wilkins, an associate director of S&P's Corparate Utilities division in London, told the briefing in Sydney that Australia's method of a gradual phasing in of the reforms was "probably better" the UK's 'big bang' method.
"In general, I see the Australian system very closely following the U.K. model," Wilkins said.
"If anything I'd say the Australian system has improved on the U.K. system, because it's realised if you're going to disaggregate you have to introduce competition at the same time," he said.
The state of Victoria had led the way in electricity privitisation, with five distributors and four generators already sold for around A$18.5 billion.
There was growing momentum for privisation in New South Wales, a market Wilkins said was twice as big as Victoria's.
NSW and Victoria had also commenced interstate trading on May 1 as part of the reform process.
Behind NSW, the states of Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania were all moving towards privatisation, and this could occur before the end of the century.

"I believe Australia is yet to reach a mature stage in the sector, and you can expect some further consolidaton between the market players and also some further M&A (merger and acquisitions) activity." Wilkins said.
"I don't know whether it's going to be as active in the U.K., but I see no reason why it shouldn't be."
One of the impacts of deregulation was that credit ratings were likely to come under downward pressure.

This was for a variety of reasons, including the loss of government guarantee and other implicit government support, exacerbated by the fact that all Australian state governments were highly rated at AAA to AA minus.

As well, following the reforms the companies were usually operating in a more competitive business environment, and the strongly competitive bidding process when the companies are intitially privatised can lead to the new entity being highly geared, Wilkins said.
"Personally, just to summarise, I think that's downwards initially," Wilkins said of the impact on credit ratings.
"I can't see things improving for any of the market, either the distributors or the generators, in the short term.
"In the medium to longer term, I think there could be improvement as some of these higly leveraged companies pay down their debt, but that's subject to debate as well."
